grammar.title: Instruções: imperativos + condicionais + time clauses
grammar.explanation_pt:
Instruções claras em inglês combinam três estruturas:

**1. Imperativos** (verbo base, sem sujeito):
- "**Hold** the lace in your right hand." / "**Don't pull** too hard." / "**Be careful not to** cut yourself."
- Com **sequenciadores**: First, ... / Then, ... / Next, ... / After that, ... / Finally, ...

**2. Zero conditional** → resultados sempre verdadeiros (como funciona):
- "If you **pull** both ends, the knot **gets** tighter."
- "When the water **boils**, the light **turns** off."

**3. First conditional** → consequências e avisos:
- "If you **tie** it this way, it **won't** come undone."
- "If you **don't** save the file, you**'ll lose** everything."

**Imperativo + if** (dicas): "**If** the app freezes, **restart** your phone." / "**If** in doubt, **ask**."

**Time clauses** (presente simples, mesmo falando do futuro):
- "**Once** you**'ve tied** the first knot, **make** a loop." (once + present perfect = depois que você tiver feito)
- "**As soon as** the light **turns** green, **press** start."
- "**Unless** the instructions **say** otherwise, **use** cold water."

rows: Don't + verbo / Be careful not to
If you press here, it opens.
If you skip this step, it won't work.

examples.en: First, cross the laces. Then, make a loop with the right lace. Be careful not to pull too hard.
examples.pt: Primeiro, cruze os cadarços. Depois, faça um laço com o cadarço direito. Cuidado para não puxar demais.

grammar.tip_pt: Em instruções escritas (manuais, receitas, tutoriais), o inglês é **direto e curto**. Não use "you should" para cada passo — o imperativo é educado nesse contexto.

reading.title: Small changes, big results
reading.text: Most of us want to be more productive, but we often look for big solutions: a new job, a new app, a complete change of routine. Productivity experts suggest the opposite. If you make small, specific changes, they'll add up over time. Here are some research-backed ideas. If you check your email first thing in the morning, you'll spend the day reacting to other people's priorities — so start with your most important task instead. When you work on a difficult task, turn off notifications: some studies suggest that it can take a long time to fully refocus after an interruption. Use the "two-minute rule": if something takes less than two minutes, do it immediately. And unless you have a very good reason, don't multitask. Our brains don't really do two things at once; they switch quickly between them, and every switch costs energy. As the saying goes, "If you chase two rabbits, you'll catch neither."

writing.model:
How to make the perfect Brazilian rice

First of all, rinse one cup of rice in cold water until the water runs clear. If you skip this step, the rice will be sticky.

Then, heat two tablespoons of oil in a pan and add half a chopped onion and one clove of garlic. Be careful not to burn the garlic — if it turns dark, it'll taste bitter.

Once the onion is soft, add the rice and stir for about two minutes. This makes the grains loose and fluffy.

Next, add two cups of hot water and a teaspoon of salt. As soon as the water boils, turn the heat down to low and cover the pan.

Cook for about 15 minutes. Don't open the lid and don't stir! When the water has disappeared and you see little holes on the surface, turn off the heat.

Finally, leave the rice covered for five more minutes. Make sure you fluff it with a fork before serving. And that's it — perfect rice, every time!

grammar.title: Obligation and advice: nuances
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você aprendeu must/have to/mustn't/don't have to. No B1+, as **nuances**:

**Must x have to (afirmativa):**
- **must** → obrigação que **o falante** sente ou impõe (interna, pessoal) e regras **escritas** formais: "I **must** call my mother — I promised." / "Passengers **must** wear seatbelts." (aviso oficial)
- **have to** → obrigação **externa** (regras, circunstâncias), mais comum na fala: "I **have to** wear a uniform at work." (a empresa exige)

**Need to / don't need to / needn't:**
- **need to** = é necessário: "We **need to** fix this bug before the launch."
- **don't need to / needn't** = não é necessário (= don't have to): "You **don't need to** bring anything." / "You **needn't** worry." (needn't é mais britânico/formal)

**Mustn't x don't have to (revisão — o erro mais comum):**
- **mustn't** = proibido: "You **mustn't** share your password."
- **don't have to / don't need to** = não é necessário: "You **don't have to** reply today."

**Should / ought to** → recomendação (o certo a fazer, mas não obrigatório):
- "You **should** proofread every email before sending it." / "We **ought to** update the checklist."

**Passado:** **had to** (obrigação), **didn't have to / didn't need to** (não era necessário), **should have** (crítica — Módulo 2).

rows: I have to submit the report by Friday.
don't have to / don't need to / needn't

grammar.tip_pt: **Need** como verbo comum pede **to** (need to do) e **do/does** nas perguntas (Do I need to...?). **Needn't** (modal) é usado sem to: "You needn't come."

reading.title: The power of checklists
reading.text: In 1935, a new American bomber plane crashed during a test flight, killing two of its crew. The investigation found that the pilots hadn't made a mechanical error — they had simply forgotten one step: they hadn't released a lock on the controls. The plane was considered "too complex for one person to fly". Instead of giving up, test pilots created a simple solution: a checklist. With it, the plane went on to fly safely for millions of miles. Decades later, surgeon and writer Atul Gawande argued in his book The Checklist Manifesto that the same idea could save lives in hospitals. A study coordinated by the World Health Organization in eight hospitals around the world found that a simple surgical safety checklist was associated with a significant reduction in complications and deaths. The checklist didn't teach surgeons anything new; it made sure that the basic steps — confirming the patient's identity, checking allergies, counting instruments — weren't overlooked. The lesson goes beyond medicine: experts don't fail because they lack knowledge, but because even the best people sometimes forget the obvious.

Rules

grammar.title: Passive voice: all tenses
grammar.explanation_pt:
No B1 você aprendeu a passiva no presente e no passado simples. A regra é sempre a mesma: **be (no tempo certo) + particípio**. Só muda o **be**:

- **Present simple:** am/is/are + particípio → "Plastic **is recycled** here."
- **Present continuous:** am/is/are **being** + particípio → "A new park **is being built**." (está sendo construído)
- **Past simple:** was/were + particípio → "The garden **was created** in 2015."
- **Past continuous:** was/were **being** + particípio → "The river **was being cleaned** when I visited."
- **Present perfect:** has/have **been** + particípio → "More than 1,000 trees **have been planted**."
- **Future (will):** will **be** + particípio → "The results **will be published** next year."
- **Going to:** am/is/are going to **be** + particípio → "The old factory **is going to be turned** into a park."
- **Modais:** can / should / must / might **be** + particípio → "Glass **can be recycled** forever." / "Food waste **should be composted**."

**Para descrever processos**, a passiva é a forma mais natural, com sequenciadores:
"First, the bottles **are collected**. Then they**'re washed** and **cut** into small pieces. After that, the pieces **are melted** and **turned** into new products."

**Get + particípio** (informal) às vezes substitui be: "My bike **got stolen**." / "The project **got cancelled**."

lines.en: Welcome to our cooperative. Let me show you how plastic bottles are recycled. First, the bottles are collected from homes and businesses by our members. Then they're sorted by color and type — this step is still done by hand. After that, the labels and caps are removed, and the bottles are washed. Next, they're cut into small flakes, which are melted and turned into pellets. reading.title: Brazil's recyclers
reading.text: In Brazil, a large part of the waste that gets recycled is collected not by machines or big companies, but by people: the catadores, or waste pickers. Estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of Brazilians work in this activity, many of them in cooperatives. For decades, their work was largely invisible and badly paid. In recent years, however, their role has been increasingly recognized. A national policy on solid waste, approved in 2010, encouraged cities to include waste picker cooperatives in their recycling systems, and in many places their work is now being formally contracted by local governments. Aluminum cans are a famous success story: Brazil has recycled a very high proportion of its aluminum cans for many years, largely thanks to the work of catadores. Challenges remain — many waste pickers still work in difficult and unsafe conditions — but their story shows that environmental solutions can't be separated from social justice.

grammar.title: Linguagem de esclarecimento
grammar.explanation_pt:
Esclarecer envolve três movimentos — e usa estruturas que você já domina (perguntas indiretas, modais, reformulação):

**1. PEDIR esclarecimento:**
- Não ouviu: "Sorry, I **didn't (quite) catch** that." / "Could you **say that again**, please?"
- Não entendeu uma palavra: "What **exactly do you mean by** 'scalable'?" / "What does '...' **mean**?"
- Quer mais detalhes: "Could you **elaborate** on that?" / "Could you **give me an example**?"
- Perguntas indiretas (mais educadas): "**I'm not sure I understand what** you mean." / "**Could you explain how** that works?"

**2. CHECAR o que você entendeu (parafrasear):**
- "**So, if I understand correctly**, you want us to...?"
- "**So what you're saying is**...?" / "**Do you mean that**...?"
- "**In other words**, ...?"

**3. DAR esclarecimento / reformular:**
- "**Let me put it another way.**" / "**What I mean is**..." / "**In plain English**, ..."
- "**To give you an example**, ..." / "**Basically**, ..." / "**The bottom line is**..."
- Checar se o outro entendeu (sem parecer arrogante): "**Does that make sense?**" / "**Is that clear?**" (cuidado: "Do you understand?" pode soar condescendente)

**Corrigir um mal-entendido com educação:**
"**Sorry, I think there's been a misunderstanding.** What I meant was..." / "**That's not quite what I meant.**"

reading.title: Lost in translation
reading.text: Misunderstandings between cultures are rarely about grammar. More often, they come from different expectations about how directly people should speak. Researchers on intercultural communication describe some cultures — like the Netherlands, Germany or Israel — as "low-context": people tend to say exactly what they mean, and the words carry most of the message. Other cultures — like Japan, China or much of Latin America, including Brazil — are often described as "high-context": a lot of the meaning comes from tone, relationships and what is not said. This can cause confusion. When a British colleague says "That's an interesting idea", they may actually mean "I don't agree". When a Brazilian says "Let's meet up sometime!", it may be a friendly expression rather than a real plan. Experts suggest a simple strategy for international teams: when in doubt, check. Paraphrase what you understood ("So you'd like me to...?"), ask for concrete details (dates, numbers, next steps) and never assume that silence means agreement.
